answer: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Special Education and Accessibility
children.blurb: A review of research on AI with students with disabilities found something uncomfortable. Much of the work described AI as a way to relieve adults of the burden of working with these students, rather than as a way to empower the students and their families (Rice, 2023).

children.name: English Learners and Newcomers
children.blurb: In a trial with 217 second graders learning English, most of them Latino, a computer tutor taught the vocabulary of science and social studies units. Students who used it learned more of the taught words than students who did not, with an effect of 0.38 (Baker et al., 2020).

children.name: Communicating With Families
children.blurb: A school district once had a problem with truancy notices. The letters sent to families were written in legal language, warning of consequences and citing the education code.

children.name: Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety
children.blurb: A study of 14 companies that monitor students online found that most watch students around the clock, not just during school hours. Most use AI to flag concerning content, but fewer than half described any human review of those flags.

children.name: Counseling, College, and Career
children.blurb: Every spring, many high school graduates are admitted to college, plan to go, and never show up in the fall. Researchers call this summer melt.

sections.body: This part of school life covers the students and families who need the most careful attention, including special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. AI in these areas is described as supporting the work around students rather than replacing the people who know them. The book presents this part as holding some of the strongest evidence in the Volume, with several randomized trials involving messages to families and support for students after high school. It also treats these chapters as places where firm rules about decisions that must stay with people apply most clearly.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, according to the book, includes messages to families and support for students after high school, which are backed by some of the strongest randomized trials in the Volume. What does not work is any arrangement that takes decisions away from people, because the book holds firm rules that certain decisions must stay with people. The rule it holds to is that AI supports the adults and families around a student, while the judgment and the decision remain human. This part also shows that careful attention to students and families is where the evidence is strongest, not weakest.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as five connected views of the same commitment to every student and every family. A teacher would go to Special Education and Accessibility and to English Learners and Newcomers for the classroom-facing work of including students who need the most careful attention. A leader would go to Communicating With Families and to Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety for the systems that keep families informed and students safe. A parent or counselor would go to Counseling, College, and Career for the path after high school, which the book ties to some of its strongest trials and to its firmest rules about decisions that stay with people.
